'''Joseph Carl Hafele''' (25 July 1933 &ndash; 15 November 2014) was an American physicist best known for the [[Hafele–Keating experiment]],<ref name=NOVA/> a test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.<ref>''Time'', October 18, 1971</ref>

Hafele was an apprentice welder when he was drafted to serve in the army during the Korean War.{{CN|date=December 2019}} After the war, he obtained undergraduate and graduate degrees from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, earning his PhD in 1962 with a thesis on a topic in nuclear physics. He married Carol Hessling in 1958, and they had four daughters. He worked at Los Alamos National Laboratory, and then [[Washington University in St. Louis]] from 1966 to 1972.<ref name=Progress/> In 1971 he performed the Hafele-Keating experiment along with astronomer [[Richard E. Keating]].<ref>''Popular Mechanics'', January 1972, p. 30</ref> He later worked at Caterpillar, [[Eureka College]], NASA ([[Langley Air Force Base]]), and [[Christopher Newport University]]. After his retirement in 1996 he and his wife lived in [[Laramie, Wyoming]], where he continued theoretical work on the interpretation of experiments that might indicate anomalies in relativity. He died in 2014 during surgery.<ref name=Progress/>
